notes.decision: Translated as 'saying' — circumstantial form of the speech-verb (Lycopolitan ⲡⲁⲭⲉ⸗ 'say'). The element ⲡ- is unclear; possibly a graphic variant or scribal artifact. The narrative function is clearly 'saying to him' introducing the disciples' question.
Direct quotation of the canonical 'good tree brings forth good fruit' (Matt 7:17 / Luke 6:43). ⲁⲛⲓⲧ = qualitative 'good/beautiful'; ϣⲁϩ+ = habitual ϣⲁϥ + 'bear/bring forth.'

Greek loanword δόγμα 'doctrine, dogma.' Plural ⲛⲁⲟⲅⲙⲁ refers to the rival philosophical-religious schools whose interpretation of the two-trees parable Mani is critiquing. Rendered 'doctrines' to preserve the technical sense of established teaching.

'Our Lord, the Anointed (Christ), the Apostle' — Mani's standard self-designation in the Kephalaia, where ⲡⲙⲛ̄ⲭⲥ (the Christ/Anointed) is applied to Mani as the Paraclete-apostle. Following the title ⲛⲧⲉ ⲧⲙⲛ̄ⲧⲛⲁⲃ ('of Greatness'), this is the canonical Manichaean apostolic formula.

ⲣ̄ϣⲉⲩ = 'be worthy/comparable'; ⲍⲟⲗⲟⲧⲉⲗⲱⲥ = Greek ὁλοτελῶς 'wholly, entirely.' The argument: the date-palm cannot stand alongside (be set together with) [the other tree] because it is not at all of equal worth — preparing Mani's rejection of a single-earth interpretation in favor of the two-root cosmology.

Rendered 'her lips and her branches.' ⲥⲟⲁⲡⲉⲧ is the Lycopolitan reflex of Sahidic ⲥⲡⲟⲧⲟⲩ 'lips' (with the prefixed ⲛⲉⲥ- read as 3fs possessive). ⲃⲁⲉ is plural of ⲃⲁ 'palm-branch.' The combination evokes a feminine personified tree-figure, fitting the ϣⲏⲛ ('tree') context of lines 6, 11. Alternative parsing ⲛⲉ-ⲥⲟⲁⲡⲉⲧ as plural article is less natural here.
'Smoke' — standard Coptic ⲕⲣⲙⲉⲥ/ⲕⲁⲡⲙⲉⲥ. The image of evil smoke arising in/before a tree fits Manichaean tree-symbolism (the Tree of Death produces smoke/darkness).

'They pronounce the verdict' — ⲧⲁⲡⲟⲫⲁⲥⲓⲥ = Greek ἀπόφασις, judicial sentence/decree. Together with ⲉⲩⲍⲁⲩ 'being evil' and ⲉⲡⲉⲓⲁⲏ 'because,' the syntax is causal: the trees are evil because the verdict is given against them.

'Whom they name' — relative ⲉⲧ- + 3pl ⲟⲩ + ϯ-ⲡⲉⲛ ('give a name'). This naming-formula recurs in line 11 (ϯⲡⲉⲛ ⲁⲣⲁⲩ ⲭⲉ ϣⲏⲛ 'they name them, saying tree') and line 33 (ⲍⲛⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲉⲩϯⲡⲉⲛ ⲁⲣⲁⲩ ⲭⲉ 'men whom they name, saying'), suggesting an exegetical pattern: 'those whom (scripture) calls X.'

'For/unto their nourishment' — ⲁ- (directional) + 3pl possessive + Greek τροφή. Likely connected with line 32 'not to touch' (ⲁⲧⲱⲙⲉ ⲉⲛ), suggesting a discussion of dietary prohibitions on the tree-fruits as electae nourishment.

'Will interpret out/forth' — future ⲛⲁ- + Greek loan ἑρμηνεύειν + ⲁⲃⲁⲗ (out, forth). The combination signals exegetical activity: 'will interpret/expound.' Confirms the page concerns scriptural exegesis of tree-imagery.
'Not to touch' — infinitive ⲁⲧ- + ⲧⲱⲙⲉ 'touch, join' + negation ⲉⲛ. Probable reference to a prohibition on touching certain things (likely the tree-fruits or types just being interpreted).

Restored '[apo]stles' on the basis of the running theme of this kephalaion (the Twelve Apostles) and the surviving final letters -ⲥⲧⲟⲗⲟⲥ. The figure being 'counted in the number of the twelve' must be Judas, who is the explicit subject of the next clause.
The fixed Lucan/Johannine formula 'Satan entered into him' (Luke 22:3 / John 13:27) is the only natural completion in this context (Judas, betrayal, the Savior delivered to the Jews).

ⲟⲩⲁⲁⲥ = Judas (Lyc. for ⲓⲟⲩⲇⲁⲥ); ⲡⲓⲥⲕⲁⲣⲓⲱⲧⲏⲥ = the Iscariot. The 'mountain' reference at the start of the line plausibly continues the preceding clause about Jesus or the disciples on a mountain, before the new sentence begins about Judas.

'A beautiful man' — ⲁⲛⲓⲧ is the qualitative of ⲁⲛⲁⲓ 'be beautiful, become good.' This contrasts with what Judas became (betrayer, murderer). The pattern parallels Paul's biography in line 7: each was 'at first' (ⲛ̄ⲱⲁⲣⲡ̄) one thing, then became another.
Greek προδότης 'betrayer' (Lyc. ⲡⲣⲟⲁⲟⲧⲏⲥ); compound ⲣⲉϥ-ϩⲱⲧⲃⲉ 'doer-of-killing' = murderer. Standard New Testament vocabulary applied to Judas.

Greek διώκτης 'persecutor' — Paul's self-description in 1 Tim 1:13 ('formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, insolent man') and parallel passages. 'Persecutor at first' establishes the Pauline mirror-image of Judas: Paul went from evil to good, Judas the reverse.
'To interpret' — the verbal form. Indicates the transition into the new chapter's hermeneutic discourse on the parable of the two trees.

ⲡⲓⲧⲱⲧ = 'the agreement, accord, harmony' (from ⲧⲱⲧ 'be joined, agreed'). Whatever the molded ones are, they are made by the consenting agreement of some power. The participle ⲁⲩⲡⲗⲁⲥⲥⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ uses Greek πλάσσειν, the technical Manichaean verb for archonic fashioning.

This appears to be the chapter heading: 'Concerning the [interp]retation of two visions (ὁράματα).' The two ὁράματα turn out (line 24-25) to be the parable of the beautiful tree and the bitter tree. ⲛⲁⲟⲣ̄ⲙⲁ = Greek ὅραμα 'vision, sight.'

'[Which the] Savior spoke in the [parable] concerning the beautiful tree and the bitter tree.' Standard Manichaean exegetical formula introducing a synoptic parable (here the two-trees logion of Matt 7:17-18 / Luke 6:43-44).

ⲙⲛ̄- here functions as the negative existential/possessive 'they have not' (knowledge); the implicit object is supplied by parallelism with line 28 ⲥⲁⲩⲛⲉ 'knowing.' Rendered 'they do not have (knowledge) that they are...' — the contrast is with those who DO know that the two trees are two distinct realities.

'The two trees are two' — the dualist thesis stated explicitly. Mani's exegesis insists that the parable indicates two ontologically distinct trees rooted in two distinct grounds (light and matter), against the monist allegorizers of single-substance doctrines.

ⲟⲩⲁⲛⲉ likely = ⲟⲩⲱⲛϩ 'manifestation, showing-forth' or possibly a term for 'branch/shoot.' Given the exegetical context ('these are X of the beautiful tree'), 'manifestation' fits as a typological identifier. Tentative — the lexeme may also denote a botanical part.

Translated 'branches' tentatively. ⲃⲁⲗⲉ here is ambiguous: it could be (a) 'eyes' (ⲃⲁⲗ) hence 'noetic eyes,' (b) palm-fronds/branches (ⲃⲁ + suffix), or (c) qualitative of ⲃⲱⲗ 'released, dissolved.' Given the surrounding tree-typology (Jesus = beautiful tree, with members and fruits), 'branches/fronds upon his body' fits best as a botanical part-of-tree term parallel to ⲕⲁⲣⲡⲟⲥ.

Translated 'producing fruit' from context. The lexeme ⲟⲩⲁϣⲙⲉ is unattested in standard Coptic lexica; possible analyses include ⲟⲩⲁϣ 'multitude' + ⲙⲉ (forming a verbal noun 'multiplying') or a compound 'in unison/abundance.' The agricultural-fruiting context with ⲕⲁⲣⲡⲟⲥ following supports a sense of multiplying/producing.

ⲡⲉϩ- is the Lycopolitan possessive prefix = Sahidic ⲡⲉϥ- 'his.' Throughout the five-faculty mapping the faculties are 'his' (= the tree's = Jesus's): his reflection, his counsel, his teaching, his thought, his mind.

Translated 'the ship of the night.' ⲧⲟⲩⲱⲏ is read as Lycopolitan variant of ⲟⲩϣⲏ 'night' — the moon-ship which carries the First Man. Parallels the 'ship of fire' (= sun, line 18) which carries the Third Ambassador. Standard Manichaean cosmology pairs sun-ship (day/fire) with Third Messenger and moon-ship (night) with First Man.

Translated 'they are conveyed upward.' The verb ⲭⲉⲥⲧ is uncertain in root but appears four times in lines 25-27 in a clear progressive pattern (catechumens → counsel → teaching → thought → mind). Possible derivations: ϫⲱϣⲧ̄ 'look,' ⲕⲱⲧⲉ 'turn,' or a transfer/conveyance verb. The pattern requires an upward-transmission semantics.

Lyc. ⲡⲱⲧ = Sahidic ⲡⲓⲱⲧ 'the Father.' Used three times on this page (lines 4, 19, 30) as the title of Jesus-as-tree (Father of apostles) and of the Father-as-Mind. Distinct from any homophone meaning 'root' or 'flight.'
Translated 'together with' from comparison with vocabulary entry ⲁⲍⲁⲛ 'near, beside.' The form ⲁϩⲁⲛ appears here as a preposition introducing 'the other mercies.'

Translated 'the great Mind of all the aeons of glory.' The Father is here identified specifically as the Great Mind (ⲡⲛⲁⲃ ⲛ̄ⲛⲟⲩⲥ) governing the totality of light-aeons. Capitalizing 'Mind' to mark the cosmological hypostatization.
Read ⲧϫⲡⲉ 'begetting, bringing forth' (cf. line 19 [ⲧ†ⲡⲉ] in the same sense). 'The flesh that walks' (ⲉⲧⲙⲁϩⲉ) likely refers to incarnate creatures.
The 'mystery' is the perverse counter-mystery placed by Satan into the cosmos — the inversion of the divine planting of the Tree of Life. The teaching of Error.

Translated 'men of wickedness' from ⲣⲙ- ('man of') + ⲃⲱⲛⲉ ('evil, vice') + ϩ. These are the human bearers of the false doctrines, the 'evil fruit' personified. Distinct from any reading 'men of life' (ⲱⲛϩ), which would invert the negative context.
Distributive doubling: 'law by law / law upon law'. Indicates the multiplicity of binding statutes in the rival systems.
ϫⲓ ϯⲡⲉ = 'receive taste / taste'; ⲁⲃⲉ = 'thirst'. Sensory verbs indicate the passional/appetitive engagement of those bound by the law of death — they consume their own poison.
ⲁⲛⲅⲣⲁⲫⲁⲩⲉ = ἀναγραφαί 'writings, records'. The clause closes the parable section: 'all the doctrines are made manifest'. Followed by 'leer' = section break.
Opens the five-membered analysis of the evil planting/Satanic body. Direct inversion of the divine five-faculty schema. Each member's negative correspondence follows in lines 30–35.

Greek μετάλλαξις/μεταλλαγμός 'exchange, alteration, transmutation'. Likely the Manichaean polemical reference to metempsychosis (transmigration of souls), here identified as the satanic counter-counsel — the 'exchange' that re-binds souls into the cycle rather than raising them.

κάμινος = 'furnace, kiln'. The negative inversion of teaching: instead of fire-of-light that purifies, the furnaces of fire that consume. The plural is significant — multiple ovens of false instruction.
γέεννα 'gehenna' filled with smoke (ⲕⲱⲣⲙⲉ = ⲕⲣⲙⲉⲥ). Negative correspondence to thought: smoke darkens and obscures perception, the inverse of clear thought.
The final dark mass (bōlos) and 'last binding' — the eschatological terminus of the satanic counter-system. Negative correspondence to mind: instead of the unifying mind, the sealed dark lump.

Greek βῶλος 'clod, lump of earth.' Translated 'clod' to preserve the chthonic-material image: damned souls bound within a lump of darkness/matter, a recurring Manichaean punishment-trope (the bōlos/sphere into which evil is sealed at the eschaton).
Reading uncertain; could be from ϣⲓⲛⲉ 'seek, ask after' (verbal noun 'seekings, inquiries'), or possibly a noun for 'fields/regions.' Translated tentatively 'seeking(?)' with question mark.
Greek καταντᾷν 'arrive at, attain' with future ⲛⲁ-. 'Will arrive at that place' fits the eschatological context (sinners reaching the place of punishment).

Greek μετάνοια 'repentance, change of mind.' The clause 'they have no repentance there' marks the irrevocability of the final judgment — standard Manichaean teaching on the fate of the damned souls in the bōlos.
Greek ἑρμηνεία 'interpretation, explanation.' Marks the formal transition from the parable (the punishment scene of lines 1–20) to its allegorical decoding: the bitter tree = matter (line 32).

This sequence appears twice (lines 25, 26). Most likely = Lycopolitan reflex of ⲛϩⲏⲧϥ/ⲛϩⲏⲧⲥ 'in him/in her', referring back to the matter (ⲍⲩⲗⲏ, fem.) or the tree. Translated 'in it.' Final ϩ may be a scribal/transcription variant for ϥ/ⲥ.
ϣⲃⲉⲓⲱ 'change, alter' fem. qualitative — 'while it is altered/changed.' Following ⲍⲛ ⲟⲩⲙⲏⲉ 'in a truth,' likely contrasts true vs. altered/false reality.

ⲕⲁⲍ = ⲕⲁϩ 'land, earth'; ⲉⲧⲁⲛⲓⲧ from ⲣ̄-ⲁⲛⲁⲓ 'be beautiful/pleasant,' qualitative ⲁⲛⲓⲧ. 'The beautiful land' = the Land of Light, contrasted with ⲡⲕⲁⲍ ⲉⲧⲍⲁⲩ 'the bitter land' (l. 34) of darkness/matter. The chapter operates by direct correspondence: bitter tree IS matter (ⲍⲩⲗⲏ) IS the bitter land of death.
Lycopolitan ⲙⲙⲁϩ = Sahidic ⲙⲙⲟϥ 'in him/it.' Final ϩ for ϥ is a regular Lycopolitan/sub-Achmimic variant.

Greek ὕλη 'matter.' This is the climactic correspondential identification of the chapter: the bitter tree IS matter. Not a comparison ('like matter') — an identity. The teaching IS the mapping: the parable's bitter tree, its bitter fruits, its bitter land, its darkness and death are all what matter IS at the cosmological register.

Feminine pronouns refer back to ⲍⲩⲗⲏ (matter, fem.). 'She herself ... upon her alone' — emphasizing matter's isolation/self-enclosure. The lacuna between ⲧⲉ and ⲙⲉ likely held a definite article ⲧ-, giving ⲧⲙⲉ 'the truth' or similar; reading uncertain.

Translated 'these two trees, originating from one another' — but lines 2-3 then deny this proposition ('they did not become from one another'). Reading the sequence as the question/thesis being refuted: the two trees (good and evil) do NOT share a common origin. Lycopolitan ⲛ̄ⲯ- = circumstantial 'as they...' or conjunctive prefix.

ⲡⲁⲣⲭⲟⲩ from Greek ὑπάρχω 'subsist, originate.' The relative ⲉⲧⲁ- introduces the contrast: 'rather, they originate (each from its own root).' The two trees of Manichaean cosmology — Tree of Life and Tree of Death — have entirely separate origins in the two principles.
ⲉⲯⲍⲁⲩ = ⲉϥϩⲁⲩ 'evil/bad.' Standard Manichaean trope: the evil tree produces the evil fruit; the good tree the good fruit. Each tree manifests according to its own root.
The doxological closing formula ϣⲁ ⲉⲛⲏϩ ⲛ̄ⲧⲉ ⲛⲉⲛⲏϩ 'forever and ever' (εἰς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων). Lycopolitan ⲏⲍⲉ for ⲏϩⲉ. This marks the close of the previous chapter on the two trees.
